item.title: How early microbial encounters shape adult behavior.
item.author: Cho KC, Lee WJ.
item.description:
Microbes are increasingly recognized as modulators of host behavior, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. A new PLOS Biology study reveals a microbiome-to-gut-to-neuron pathway linking developmental microbial exposure to later food avoidance.
Citation and preview: Europe PMC. Publisher access terms apply.

item.title: Rethinking neurodegeneration: Placing disease in its physiological context.
item.author: Clarke J, Jäkel S.
item.description:
Research into neurodegeneration is often confined to a single disease, cell type or mechanism. A new collection of articles explores neurodegeneration within its physiological context, looking beyond diseased neurons to the surrounding tissue microenvironment.
Citation and preview: Europe PMC. Publisher access terms apply.

item.title: Viral disease outcomes are indistinguishable between experimentally infected bats and rodents.
item.author: Farrell MJ, Tucker SK, Mollentze N, Streicker DG.
item.description:
A common explanation for bats being a conspicuous source of zoonotic viruses is their purported ability to coexist with viruses without suffering overt disease. Widespread acceptance of the idea that bats have unusual antiviral traits has catalyzed the discovery of unique features of bat immune systems which may have translational value as broad-spectrum antivirals, particularly if they evolved as a byproduct of bats' unique life history rather than through conventional co-evolutionary processes. Surprisingly, whether bats compared to other host groups suffer less disease from co-evolved viruses or from viruses generally has not been formally assessed. item.title: Full-length genomes evolve in parallel in a long-term evolution experiment with phage φX174.
item.author: Bons E, Chabas H, MacDonald H, Escalera Ledermann A, Ösze S, Dunstan J, Ochsner N, Angst DC, Bonhoeffer S, Regoes RR.
item.description:
The study of evolution in organisms with high mutation rates requires detailed data on the genomic composition of the population. Here we report on an innovative use of high-throughput sequencing technology combined with rapid experimental evolution that allowed us to follow the genetic diversification of four independent bacteriophage populations for 412 generations in extraordinary detail. One of our goals was to assess phylodynamic methods that use genetic information to infer key parameters of the population history. Because phylodynamic methods assume neutral evolution, we did not actively impose any selection pressures in our evolution experiment (in addition to those inherent in the bacterial cell environment). item.title: Transient feedforward communication between somatosensory and premotor cortex supports goal-directed behavior.
item.author: Ranjbar-Slamloo Y, Kamigaki T.
item.description:
Goal-directed behavior requires sensory information to be transformed into motor commands, yet the precise temporal structure of communication between sensory and motor cortices during this process remains poorly understood. By simultaneously recording spiking activity from primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and secondary motor cortex (M2) in mice performing a tactile delayed go/no-go task, we identified a brief, stimulus-triggered communication window that predicted behavioral success. Time-shifted canonical correlation analysis revealed a sharp, feedforward surge in S1 → M2 coupling peaking at a short latency, as expected for a potentially direct transmission pathway. This transient interaction conveyed stimulus-selective information such that the S1 → M2 communication subspace aligned with stimulus-coding axes in both regions. item.title: Alzheimer's disease research must connect vascular molecular phenotypes with physiology.
item.author: Lewis TS, Wagner J, Neher JJ.
item.description:
Molecular profiling studies have mapped vascular alterations in Alzheimer's disease, but have not proven a role for them in pathology. Longitudinal studies are needed to link molecular and structural changes to vascular mechanics, hemodynamics, and tissue perfusion.
Citation and preview: Europe PMC. Publisher access terms apply.

item.title: Conserved spike epitopes persist in generalist bat sarbecoviruses.
item.author: Frieman MB.
item.description:
Bat sarbecoviruses differ in the range of mammalian ACE2 receptors they can use, complicating predictions of spillover risk. Two new studies in PLOS Biology link receptor breadth with antigenic relatedness and reveal conserved spike epitopes targetable by antibodies.

item.title: Pollinator abundance shapes sexual selection in an angiosperm.
item.author: Barbot E, Dufaÿ M, Janicke T, Lapeyre B, Orcel D, Rousset F, Tonnabel J.
item.description:
Sexual selection is a central force in evolutionary biology that has been shown to shape phenotypes and population dynamics in animals. While this selective force is increasingly recognized in flowering plants, theory predicts that anisogamy generates sex differences in the fitness benefits of acquiring additional mates-a pattern well supported in animals but with limited tests in plants. Plant studies rely solely on genetic parentage analyses to estimate mate numbers, thereby conflating performance in accessing mates with success in gamete fertilization. Pollinators add an ecological layer, as their behavior and abundance can influence competition for access to mates and their gametes. item.title: fruitless is essential for male Aedes aegypti mosquito attraction to female flight sounds.
item.author: Loh YM, Thornton AJ, Loh W, Lee TT, Chen WT, Xu YYJ, Yap JX, Tsuchiya Y, Eberl DF, Su MP, Kamikouchi A.
item.description:
Male mosquitoes locate females through strong and innate attraction to female flight sounds, the basis of mating in the world's deadliest animal. In contrast, females do not show any sound attraction behaviors. Despite being documented for almost a century, the molecular underpinnings of these behavioral dimorphisms remain unknown. Here, we found that by disrupting the male-specific isoform of fruitless (referred to as fruM) in Aedes aegypti, fruM mutant males show complete abolition of sound attraction behaviors, resulting in failure of mutant males to locate females for mating.
